content_voiceover: This slide introduces tissue factor pathway inhibitor, or TFPI, the natural brake on the initiation phase. TFPI first binds and inhibits factor ten a, then that TFPI ten a complex docks onto the tissue factor seven a complex, forming an inhibitory quaternary complex that shuts down the extrinsic tenase. You can see the X marks over nine a and ten a on the left, showing that further activation of factor nine and factor ten by this pathway is now blocked. This is exactly why the extrinsic pathway can only ever generate a small initial burst of thrombin, not sustained clot formation. Meanwhile, on the right side of the slide, you can see that the small amount of thrombin already generated is starting to feed back and activate factor eight and factor five, setting the stage for the intrinsic tenase and full prothrombinase complexes that will drive propagation.
keypoints: TFPI binds factor ten a, then docks onto tissue factor seven a
This quaternary complex shuts down further extrinsic tenase activity
TFPI limits initiation to a brief, self-terminating burst
Early thrombin feeds back to activate factors five and eight for propagation
keypoint_voiceover: TFPI's mechanism is two step: it grabs ten a, then that complex parks on tissue factor seven a and switches the extrinsic tenase off. That's why initiation is self limited, and why sustaining clot formation requires the thrombin feedback loop that activates factors five and eight.
